study_identification.title: Capturing the Individual Deviations From Normative Models of Brain Structure for Depression Diagnosis and Treatment

study_characteristics.study_objective: To investigate clinical issues related to depression according to individual deviations from normative ranges of gray matter volume, with the aim of developing individualized diagnosis and treatment approaches for depression.

site_effect_handling_detail.reason:
The paper provides detailed description of site effect handling using ComBat. The Harmonization section in Methods states: 'To minimize the nonbiological variance introduced by differences in MRI scanners and acquisition protocols, we used the ComBat method to harmonize data from these three datasets'. It further explains: 'Specifically, we first harmonized the data from dataset I (discovery cohort) and datasets II and III into a common domain using the ComBat method. To avoid a potential data leakage problem for subsequent classification modeling, we retained the biological variability related to age, sex, and TIV, without preserving the diagnostic labels. Then, the pretrained ComBat model was applied to harmonize the external test set directly'. The batch variables are implicitly the scanner/site differences between the three datasets acquired on different Siemens scanners.
EXTRAS: {"value": "ComBat harmonization method was used to minimize nonbiological variance introduced by differences in MRI scanners and acquisition protocols across three datasets. The discovery cohort (Dataset I) and normative datasets (II and III) were harmonized into a common domain while preserving biological variability related to age, sex, and TIV but not diagnostic labels to avoid data leakage. The pretrained ComBat model was then applied to harmonize the external test set."}
site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: To minimize the nonbiological variance introduced by differences in MRI scanners and acquisition protocols, we used the ComBat method to harmonize data from these three datasets. ComBat is a popular batch adjustment method developed for genomics expression analysis that has been demonstrated to remove the unwanted variation introduced by site in diffusion tensor imaging or structural MRI studies, while effectively preserving biological variability. Specifically, we first harmonized the data from dataset I (discovery cohort) and datasets II and III into a common domain using the ComBat method. To avoid a potential data leakage problem for subsequent classification modeling, we retained the biological variability related to age, sex, and TIV, without preserving the diagnostic labels. Then, the pretrained ComBat model was applied to harmonize the external test set directly.

clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Normative modeling revealed highly individualized patterns of gray matter abnormalities in depression (less than 11% patient overlap for any region), with diagnostic models based on normative deviations outperforming models using raw GMV values (AUC 0.71-0.78 vs. 0.68-0.70 in discovery; 0.61-0.74 vs. 0.56-0.61 in external test set), and distinct latent brain structural factors associated with SSRI treatment response and medication type selection.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The study found that 92.91% of depression patients showed extreme deviations in at least one brain region, but for any single region, less than 11% of patients deviated from the normative range, demonstrating substantial individual heterogeneity. In the discovery cohort, classification models trained with normative probability maps (NPMs) consistently outperformed models trained with original GMV values across different SVM kernels (AUC range 0.7146-0.7836 vs. 0.6800-0.7036), with the best performance achieved using RBF kernel with feature selection and ComBat harmonization. This superiority was validated in an independent external test set (AUC 0.6063-0.7396 vs. 0.5613-0.6089). Feature analysis identified 36 brain regions selected in more than 5000/10,000 iterations, with 9 regions (bilateral rolandic operculum, right olfactory cortex, left insula, left fusiform gyrus, left pallidum, left Heschl gyrus, left superior temporal gyrus, left inferior temporal gyrus) selected in >9000 iterations. Treatment-related analysis using pLDA revealed that SSRI responders tended to express Factor 2 (associated with reduced GMV in frontal-parietal, subcortical, limbic, and temporal areas), while non-responders mainly expressed Factor 3 (associated with increased GMV in frontal-parietal and occipital areas). When comparing medication types among responders, patients targeted by SSRIs mainly expressed Factor 1, while those targeted by SNRIs mainly expressed Factor 3, suggesting distinct neurobiological profiles associated with different antidepressant mechanisms. Notably, conventional case-control analysis found only 9 of 90 brain regions with significantly lower GMV in depression patients in the discovery cohort (FDR p<0.05), and no significant differences were found in the external test set, highlighting the advantage of individual-level normative modeling over group-level comparisons.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: First, the normative age modeling was based on cross-sectional data and should be validated with longitudinal data to make claims about trajectories at the individual level. Second, the study focused on patients between 18 and 65 years of age, limiting applicability to late-life depression or adolescent depression. Finally, more subtype samples could be added to the normative model to mine subtype specificity by observing cluster characteristics of NPM.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The authors suggest that individual deviation maps could be used in the future to delineate more putative biological subtypes or provide more detailed personalized treatment options, moving toward precision medicine. The study demonstrates that capturing personalized deviations from normative ranges can help diagnose depression at an individual level and provide guidance on treatment options. The pLDA findings regarding medication-specific brain structural patterns suggest potential for pre-treatment stratification to guide antidepressant selection between SSRIs and SNRIs.

general_notes.general_notes: This study represents a comprehensive application of normative modeling to depression, including not only diagnostic classification but also treatment-related analyses. The use of ComBat harmonization prior to normative modeling is notable, as it addresses site/scanner effects at the data level before building the normative model. The study employs B-spline Bayesian linear regression implemented in PCNtoolkit, which allows for flexible non-linear age modeling while accounting for both data uncertainty and modeling uncertainty in deviation scores. The extensive resampling approach (10,000 iterations) for classification modeling with rigorous statistical testing (k-fold CV paired t-test, 5×2 CV F-test, DeLong's test) strengthens the validity of the diagnostic findings. The application of polar LDA to treatment-related questions is innovative, discretizing z-scores to enable topic modeling approaches and distinguishing between hyper- and hypo-GMV patterns. The study demonstrates clear advantages of normative modeling over traditional case-control approaches: while only 9/90 regions showed significant group differences in the discovery cohort (and none in the external test set), the individual-level normative deviations enabled successful diagnostic classification in both cohorts. The treatment-related findings suggest that responders to SSRIs show patterns of reduced GMV in frontal-parietal, subcortical, and limbic regions, while non-responders show increased GMV in frontal-parietal and occipital regions, which may reflect different underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. The convergence of factors across different pLDA models (correlations 0.85-0.94 between medication efficacy and medication type models) provides validation of the identified latent structural patterns. Datasets: Human Connectome Project (HCP) n=510 participants aged 22-36 from multiple sites; REST-meta-MDD Project site 20, n=229 participants aged 18-65; local clinical cohorts from two hospitals in China (Affiliated Brain Hospital of Nanjing Medical University and Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital). All data acquired on Siemens 3T scanners. Treatment protocol: antidepressant monotherapy for 4 weeks with dosages following Chinese depression treatment guidelines; responders defined as ≥50% reduction in HAMD-17 scores. Some patients also received ECT (n=33) but those patients were excluded from the medication-only treatment analysis (n=154 for pLDA analyses).
